newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. special envoy Sahnoun to Uganda over Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. special envoy Sahnoun to Uganda over Zaire.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun flew to Uganda on Friday for talks with Uganda President and regional power broker Yoweri Museveni on the war in Zaire, diplomats said.

They said Sahnoun, a joint envoy of the United Nations and Organisation of African Unity, would meet Museveni in the northern Ugandan town of Gulu where the president is supervising a counter-offensive against rebels.
On Thursday last week, Sahnoun met Museveni and Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila at Gulu, a remote northern outpost, where Kabila rejected Sahnoun's plea for a ceasefire in Zaire.
Sahnoun was later in the day expected fly to Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, for talks with Kabila to attempt to secure a ceasefire to pave the way for negogitations.
"He (Sahnoun) has gone to Uganda for talks with Museveni and will go to Kisangani to meet Kabila," a diplomat told Reuters.

Another diplomat said talks with Museveni and Kabila would centre on securing a ceasefire and would examine Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's position that he does not rule out talks with the rebels.

Mobutu, who left hospital in Monaco on Wednesday after fresh cancer treatment, called on Thursday for a truce in an eve-of-departure statement issued from his villa in the south of France and for a national council to find a peace settlement.
Kabila, expected in Kisangani later on Friday from his headquarters at Goma, has yet to respond to Mobutu's offer but he has previously demanded negotiations before any ceasefire.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) has seized more than one-fifth of Zaire since October. Kabila says he wants only face-to-face talks with Mobutu or his representative to decide how he will stand down.
Mobutu's son, Nzanga, said in France on Thursday his father no longer ruled out talks with the rebels but wanted to involve the government, army and transitional parliament.

Mobutu, 66, has spent almost all his time in Europe since having prostate cancer surgery in August. He has dominated Zaire with a mix of political acumen and military ruthlessness since seizing power in 1965.
The diplomats said Sahnoun's talks with Museveni aimed at persuading the Ugandan leader, accused by Zaire of backing Kabila, to press the rebels for a ceasefire in light of Mobutu's statement.
They said, depending on the outcome of talks with Museveni and Kabila, Sahnoun might take his diplomatic shuttle to Kinshasa where Mobutu was expected to arrive from France later on Friday.

The rebel force is dominated by ethnic Tutsis, some of them Zairean Banyamulenge Tutsis and others said by intelligence sources to be members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army. The Rwandan government denies any involvement with the rebels.
Demobilised Ugandan troops, hired on contract, are also part of the rebel force. Kabila is a Zairean non-Tutsi from Shaba and his field commanders are a mixture of Zaireans and foreigners.
